I looked at the real crime data for every town on this list, and the numbers are worse than the brochures admit. We're talking about the #1 town with a violent-crime rate more than 6.5x the national average and a poverty rate near one in three, a beloved beach town whose property crime tops 5,600 per 100,000, a town that produced a NASA astronaut and a national arts festival yet still can't outrun its crime charts, and a Fortune 500 headquarters sitting minutes from entrenched violence. This is 12 South Carolina Towns So Dangerous Even Locals Avoid Them After Dark, counted down to the single most dangerous at #1, Dillon, the little Interstate 95 town hiding behind that world-famous neon sombrero.

— #12 Florence: violent crime around 807 per 100,000 (about 2.5x the national average) and property crime near 3,900, driven by the I-95/I-20 junction that funnels traffic and trouble through the Pee Dee.
— #11 North Charleston: violent crime near 810 per 100,000 (about 126% above national) in the state's third-largest city, where the 2015 Walter Scott shooting made national news and a Boeing boomtown shares one name with a high-crime city.
— #10 Marion: property crime near 5,300 per 100,000 (roughly triple national) in a poor, flood-battered county seat where Hurricanes Matthew and Florence swallowed nearby Nichols twice in two years.
— #9 Bennettsville: violent crime around 995 per 100,000 (about 177% above national) in the county seat of Marlboro, ranked one of the poorest counties in the state year after year.
— #8 Sumter: violent crime around 1,098 per 100,000 (more than 3x national) even with Shaw Air Force Base's steady federal payroll and the famous Swan Lake Iris Gardens.
— #7 Myrtle Beach: property crime near 5,656 per 100,000 (over 3x national) on the Grand Strand, though the rate is measured against roughly 34,000 permanent residents, not the summer crowds.
— #6 Darlington: violent crime around 1,131 per 100,000 and total crime above 7,000 in a town of about 6,000 that only fills up on NASCAR race weekends.
— #5 Orangeburg: violent crime around 1,246 per 100,000 (nearly 250% above national) and property crime above 6,000, in a town anchored by two historically Black universities and the 1968 Orangeburg Massacre.
— #4 Chester: violent crime around 1,554 per 100,000 (about 333% above national) in a beautiful hilltop textile town of roughly 5,500 where the mills left but the violence stayed.
— #3 Hartsville: violent crime around 1,746 per 100,000 (nearly 5x national) in a town under 8,000 that is home to Coker University and Fortune 500 packaging giant Sonoco.
— #2 Lake City: violent crime around 1,802 per 100,000 (roughly 5x national) in the under-7,000-person birthplace of Challenger astronaut Ronald McNair and the ArtFields festival.
— #1 Dillon: violent crime about 2,372 per 100,000 (more than 6.5x national, over 400% above the state average), total crime past 9,000, and a Census poverty rate around 32.8% with median household income near $35,000.
— The honest caveat repeated all night: every figure is a citywide average, and averages hide the safe, comfortable streets sitting right alongside the rough ones.

videos.description:
#WeirdSouthCarolina #SouthCarolina #Retirement 

South Carolina's tourism board would pay actual money to make sure you never see this video — not because these towns are dangerous, but because once you realize there's a community in this state where the United States Air Force accidentally dropped a nuclear bomb on a family's backyard and the government's settlement was $54,000, that there's an incorporated town here with the legal name Ninety Six that has been on official maps since the colonial era and was the site of the first land battle of the American Revolution in the South, that a man with zero horticultural training built one of the most internationally recognized private sculpture gardens in America from plants rescued off a nursery's trash pile while a few miles away another man covered his house, his car, and his coffin in over 600,000 hand-sewn buttons because he couldn't sleep — and that a 135-foot water tower shaped like an anatomically detailed peach has been causing involuntary double-takes on Interstate 85 since 1981 — you start to wonder whether the whole state just collectively lost its mind at some point and nobody told you. Number two on this list is a place that made me pull over and read the sign three times. If this video gets 50,000 likes, I'll do a part two. South Carolina has more than enough material. Let's count it down.

📌 TOPICS COVERED

Hollywood, Sugar Tit, Due West, Forty Five — communities named before anyone thought to ask whether posterity would find the choice strange; Hollywood SC predates California's version and sits twenty miles outside Charleston in the ACE Basin marshes; Sugar Tit's name is antebellum and entirely wholesome in origin; Due West's name is either a directional reference or a corruption of DeWitt's Corner, and historians have never settled which
Pelion, Ridgeway, Johnston, Gaffney — Midlands and Upstate towns defined by one thing they refuse to let go of; Pelion's annual Peanut Party draws tens of thousands to a town of 800; Ridgeway's police station is a repurposed structure roughly the dimensions of a phone booth; Johnston is the self-proclaimed Peach Capital of the World with USDA production numbers that back the claim; Gaffney's Peachoid is a one-million-gallon water tower that starred in House of Cards after causing a documented spike in deliberate tourism
Ninety Six, Bishopville, Mars Bluff — where South Carolina history gets genuinely unsettling; the Ninety Six National Historic Site (a free National Park Service unit) preserves the earthworks of the first land battle of the American Revolution in the South; Pearl Fryar's three-acre topiary garden in Bishopville was built from nursery discards by a man with no training, called the Picasso of Plants by Smithsonian Magazine; the Button King Museum holds more than 600,000 hand-sewn buttons across a car, a coffin, and a house; Mars Bluff's 1958 nuclear bomb impact left a 70-foot crater and a $54,000 federal settlement — the crater is still visible today
South Carolina's retiree and visitor picture — Social Security income is exempt from SC state income tax; cost of living in these small towns runs well below the national average; the Ninety Six National Historic Site is free to visit
An honest note: most of these communities have populations under 3,000 with limited retail, medical, and dining infrastructure; Pearl Fryar passed away in 2024 and the garden is now maintained by a foundation — verify hours before visiting
